title: The Invention of Paper
summary: How paper was invented in ancient China, how the craft of papermaking was made, and how it slowly traveled west to the Islamic world and on to Europe.
poll: Learning how to make something is just as important as inventing it in the first place.

versions.title: The Invention of Paper
versions.text:
Long ago, there was no paper. People wrote on skin or bone. They used leaves too.

In China, a man made a new craft. He used old cloth, bark, and bits of plant. He mixed it with water. This wet mix is pulp.

He put the pulp on a screen. It was thin and flat. Water ran out of it. Then he pressed it flat. He let it dry in the sun. It was paper!

Paper was light. It was cheap. It was easy to write on.

For a long time, only China knew this craft. Other lands did not know it yet.

Slow traders went west. They used old trade roads. The craft went with them. It reached a city called Samarkand.

Then it went on. It reached Baghdad. Workers there built mills. They made the pulp fine. The paper got strong.

In time, the craft reached Spain. Then it went to the rest of Europe.

One small craft went a long way. Each place made it a bit better.

Long ago, there was no paper at all. People wrote on animal skin, bone, or palm leaves.

In China, a man made a new craft long ago. He used old cloth, tree bark, and bits of plant. He mixed it all with water. This made a soft, wet mix called pulp.

He spread the wet pulp in a thin layer. He used a flat screen. Water dripped out through the screen. Then he pressed it flat. He let it dry in the sun. It dried into a thin, light sheet. It was paper!

This new craft was a big deal. Paper was light. It was easy to carry. It was cheap to make. It was easy to write on too.

For a long time, China kept this craft close to home. Few people outside China knew the steps to make it.

Slowly, over many years, traders carried the craft west. It went along old trade roads. It reached far cities such as Samarkand.

From there, the craft spread on. It reached Baghdad and other busy cities. Workers built paper mills there. They used rags to make the pulp fine. The paper got much stronger.

In time, the craft reached Spain in the west. From Spain, it crossed into the rest of Europe.

One simple craft went all the way from China to Europe. Each place that learned it made it a little better.

From there, papermaking kept spreading. It reached Baghdad, Damascus, and other busy cities. Skilled workers set up a paper workshop in each city, using rags and flowing water to make the pulp finer. The trade began to flourish, and the paper grew much stronger.

In time, the craft reached Spain in the west, and mills were built in cities such as Xativa. From Spain, papermaking slowly crossed into the rest of Europe, reaching towns in Italy by the 1200s.

Long ago, there was no paper at all. People wrote on animal skin, bone, or palm leaves instead, and none of these materials were cheap or easy to obtain in large quantities.

In ancient China, a court official named Cai Lun is traditionally credited with refining a new craft around two thousand years ago, during the Han dynasty. Workers used old cloth, tree bark, hemp, and other plant fiber. They mashed these materials together with water into a soft, wet mixture called pulp.

They spread the wet pulp in a thin, even layer across a flat screen called a mold. Water drained out through tiny holes in the screen, leaving a damp mat of fiber behind. Workers then pressed the thin layer flat and left it to dry in the sun or open air. It dried into a thin, lightweight sheet of paper, ready for writing.

This new craft turned out to be an enormously significant development for the whole world. Paper was light and easy to transport from one place to another. It was fairly inexpensive to produce from common plants and discarded cloth. It was also smooth and pleasant to write on, unlike rough animal skin.

For several centuries, China kept this valuable craft largely secret, and very few people outside the country knew the exact steps required to make good paper.

Gradually, over many years, traders and travelers carried the skill westward along ancient trade roads. The craft eventually reached far cities such as Samarkand in Central Asia, where local workers learned the technique for themselves.

From Samarkand, papermaking continued spreading steadily. It reached Baghdad, Damascus, and other busy cities throughout the Islamic world, where each city built its own paper workshop. Skilled workers used linen rags and flowing river water to refine the pulp, and the trade began to flourish, producing paper considerably stronger than before.

In time, the craft reached Spain in the west, and mills were established in cities such as Xativa. From Spain, papermaking gradually crossed into the rest of Europe, reaching Italian towns such as Fabriano by the 1200s.

One simple craft traveled all the way from China to Europe over many hundreds of years. Each new place that learned the craft refined it a little further along the way, adding its own local improvements.

versions.title: The Invention of Paper: A Craft That Traveled
versions.text:
Long ago, no paper existed anywhere in the world. People wrote on animal skin, bone, or palm leaves instead, materials that were neither cheap nor easy to obtain in the amounts that writing required.

In China, a court official named Cai Lun is traditionally credited with refining the craft of papermaking around 105 CE, during the Han dynasty, although simpler forms of paper likely existed a bit earlier. Workers soaked old cloth, tree bark, hemp, and other plant fiber, then beat these materials with water into a soft, wet mixture called pulp.

Workers spread the wet pulp in a thin, even layer across a flat screen known as a mold. Water drained through tiny holes in the screen, leaving behind a damp mat of tangled fiber. The thin layer was then pressed to squeeze out more moisture before drying in the sun or open air. It emerged as a thin, light sheet of paper, ready for writing.

This innovation was a hugely important exchange of knowledge with the whole world. Paper was light and easy to transport, cheap to produce from common plants and discarded cloth, and smooth and pleasant to write upon, unlike rough animal skin or heavy clay tablets.

For several centuries, China guarded this valuable craft closely, and very few people beyond its borders understood the exact technique needed to produce good paper.

Gradually, over many generations, traders and travelers carried the skill west along ancient trade routes through Central Asia, and the craft reached distant cities such as Samarkand, where local artisans adapted the technique for themselves.

From Samarkand, papermaking kept spreading through the Islamic world, reaching Baghdad, Damascus, and Cairo. Skilled workers set up a paper workshop in each of these busy cities, using linen rags and flowing river water to refine the pulp further. The craft began to flourish, producing paper considerably stronger and smoother than earlier versions.

In time, the craft reached Spain in the far west, where mills were built in cities such as Xativa during the eleventh and twelfth centuries. From Spain, papermaking crossed into the rest of Europe, reaching Italian towns such as Fabriano by the 1200s and spreading further across the continent afterward.

One simple craft, born in China, traveled an immense distance to reach Europe over many hundreds of years, and each region that adopted it left its own legacy of small improvements along the way.

versions.title: The Invention of Paper: A Craft That Traveled
versions.text:
Long ago, no paper existed anywhere in the world, and people instead wrote upon animal skin, bone, or palm leaves—materials that proved neither inexpensive nor readily obtainable in the quantities that writing and record-keeping increasingly demanded as societies grew more complex and administratively sophisticated.

In ancient China, a court official named Cai Lun is traditionally credited with refining the craft of papermaking around the year 105 CE, during the Han dynasty, although simpler forms of paper likely existed somewhat earlier than this traditional date suggests, developed gradually through the efforts of unnamed artisans working over generations. Workers soaked old cloth, tree bark, hemp, and other plant fiber, then beat these raw materials together with water into a soft, saturated mixture known as pulp, the essential starting point from which every subsequent sheet would be formed.

Workers spread the wet pulp in a thin, remarkably even layer across a flat screen known as a mold, specially designed and shaped for this exact purpose. Water drained steadily through countless tiny holes in the screen, leaving behind a damp, tangled mat of interwoven fiber. This thin layer was then pressed firmly to squeeze out any remaining moisture, before being left to dry thoroughly in the sun or open air, ultimately emerging as a thin, lightweight sheet of finished paper, ready for writing or further trimming to size.

This innovation proved to be an enormously significant exchange of knowledge for civilizations spanning the entire world. Paper was lightweight and remarkably easy to transport across long distances, inexpensive to produce from common plants and discarded cloth rags, and remarkably smooth and pleasant to write upon, quite unlike rough animal skin or heavy, breakable clay tablets that preceded it.

For several centuries, China guarded this valuable craft rather closely as something approaching a national secret, and very few people beyond its borders understood the precise technique required to produce good paper consistently, reliably, and at any meaningful scale.

Gradually, over many generations, traders and travelers carried the skill westward along ancient trade routes that crossed the vast expanse of Central Asia, and the craft eventually reached distant cities such as Samarkand, where local artisans skillfully adapted the technique for their own available materials, tools, and climate.

From Samarkand, papermaking continued spreading steadily throughout the wider Islamic world, reaching Baghdad, Damascus, and Cairo in turn, with each city contributing its own particular expertise to the evolving craft. Skilled workers established bustling paper mills within these cities, using linen rags and flowing river water, often harnessed deliberately by waterwheels, to refine the pulp still further, thereby producing paper considerably stronger and smoother than any earlier version had managed to be.

In time, the craft reached Spain in the far west, where mills were established in cities such as Xativa during the eleventh and twelfth centuries. From Spain, papermaking gradually crossed into the rest of Europe, reaching Italian towns such as Fabriano by the 1200s and spreading steadily further across the continent in the centuries that followed its initial arrival there.

One simple craft, born in ancient China, traveled an immense distance to reach Europe over many hundreds of years, and each new region that adopted the technique left its own legacy of local refinements and quiet innovations on the overall process, slowly shaping the paper that people everywhere still rely upon today.

versions.title: The Invention of Paper: A Craft That Traveled
versions.text:
Long ago, no paper existed anywhere in the world, and people instead wrote upon animal skin, bone, or palm leaves—materials that proved neither inexpensive nor readily obtainable in the quantities that writing and record-keeping increasingly demanded as societies grew more complex and administratively sophisticated over time.

In ancient China, a court official named Cai Lun is traditionally credited with refining the craft of papermaking around the year 105 CE, during the Han dynasty, although simpler, cruder forms of paper likely existed somewhat earlier than this conventional date suggests, developed gradually and anonymously through the accumulated efforts of unnamed artisans working across several generations. Workers methodically soaked old cloth, tree bark, hemp, and other plant fiber, then thoroughly beat these raw materials together with water into a soft, saturated mixture known as pulp, the essential starting point from which every subsequent sheet would eventually be formed.

Workers spread the wet pulp in an extraordinarily thin, remarkably even layer across a flat screen known as a mold, specially designed and precisely shaped for this exact purpose. Water drained steadily through countless tiny perforations in the screen, leaving behind a damp, tangled mat of densely interwoven fiber. This thin layer was then pressed firmly and deliberately to squeeze out any remaining moisture, before being left to dry thoroughly in the sun or open air, ultimately emerging as a thin, lightweight sheet of finished paper, ready for writing or further trimming to a desired size.

This innovation proved to be an enormously significant exchange of knowledge for civilizations spanning the entire inhabited world. Paper was lightweight and remarkably easy to transport across considerable distances, comparatively inexpensive to produce from common plants and discarded cloth rags, and remarkably smooth and pleasant to write upon, quite unlike the rough animal skin or heavy, breakable clay tablets that had preceded it for centuries.

For several centuries thereafter, China guarded this valuable craft rather closely as something approaching a closely held national secret, and precious few people beyond its borders ever understood the precise technique required to produce good paper consistently, reliably, and at any truly meaningful scale.

Gradually, over many successive generations, traders and travelers carried the skill steadily westward along ancient trade routes that crossed the vast expanse of Central Asia, and the craft eventually reached distant cities such as Samarkand, where resourceful local artisans skillfully adapted the technique to suit their own available materials, tools, and regional climate.

From Samarkand, papermaking continued spreading steadily throughout the wider Islamic world, eventually reaching Baghdad, Damascus, and Cairo in succession, with each city contributing its own particular expertise and refinements to the continuously evolving craft. Skilled workers methodically established bustling paper mills within these cities, employing linen rags and flowing river water, frequently harnessed deliberately by ingenious waterwheels, to refine the pulp still further, thereby producing paper considerably stronger and smoother than any earlier version had previously managed to achieve.

In time, the craft reached Spain in the far west, where dedicated mills were established in cities such as Xativa during the eleventh and twelfth centuries. From Spain, papermaking gradually crossed into the remainder of Europe, eventually reaching Italian towns such as Fabriano by the 1200s and spreading steadily further across the continent in the centuries that subsequently followed its initial arrival there.

One simple craft, originally born in ancient China, traveled an immense and improbable distance to eventually reach Europe over many hundreds of years, and each new region that adopted the technique left its own legacy of local refinements and quiet innovations on the overall process along the way, slowly and collectively shaping the paper that people everywhere still rely upon today.

keyWords.definition: a skill used to make something by hand
keyWords.example: Weaving baskets is a craft my grandmother taught me.

keyWords.definition: a soft, wet mix made by mashing cloth or plants with water
keyWords.example: The workers turned old rags into soft, wet pulp.

keyWords.definition: to push down hard on something to flatten it or squeeze out water
keyWords.example: She had to press the clay flat with her hands.

keyWords.definition: a building with machines where something is made or ground
keyWords.example: Workers at the mill ground wheat into flour.

keyWords.definition: to lose water and become hard or stiff
keyWords.example: We let the wet clothes dry in the sun.

questions.stem: What is this article mostly about?
options: How animals are trained to carry goods across a desert
How the craft of making paper was invented and spread
How to paint pictures with bright colors
How mosques are built in old cities
questions.why: The article tells how paper was first made in China and how the craft spread to other lands.

wrong.A: Animals are not discussed in this article.
wrong.C: Painting is not the topic of the article.
wrong.D: Mosques are not mentioned in the article.

questions.stem: What did people write on before paper was invented?
options: Plastic sheets and large panes of glass
Large, heavy cotton blankets sewn together
Thin sheets of gold hammered by hand
Animal skin, bone, or dried palm leaves
questions.why: The article says people wrote on animal skin, bone, or palm leaves before paper was made.

wrong.A: Plastic and glass did not exist that long ago.
wrong.C: Gold sheets are not mentioned as writing material.

questions.stem: What is pulp in the article?
options: A soft, wet mix of cloth and plant with water
A thin, dry, finished sheet of paper
A special tool used only to press paper flat
An old kind of material made from animal skin
questions.why: The article says pulp is the soft, wet mix made by mashing cloth and plant parts with water.

wrong.B: The dry sheet comes after the pulp, not before.
wrong.C: A press is a tool, not the mix itself.
wrong.D: Animal skin was used before paper, but it is not pulp.

questions.stem: Why did workers spread the wet pulp onto a screen?
options: To hide the wet pulp from people in other cities
To make the wet pulp heavier and harder to dry
To let water drip out and leave a thin layer
To add a bright new color to the pulp mixture
questions.why: Spreading pulp on a screen let the water drain away, leaving a thin layer that could dry into paper.

wrong.A: Hiding the pulp is not mentioned.
wrong.B: Draining water makes the layer lighter, not heavier.

questions.stem: Why was paper such a big deal when it was first made?
options: It was heavy, rough, and hard to carry around
It was light, cheap, and easy to write on
It could only ever be used just one single time
It always cost far more than animal skin did
questions.why: The article says paper was light, cheap to make, and easy to write on, unlike older materials.

wrong.A: The article says paper was light, not heavy.
wrong.C: The article does not say paper could only be used once.
wrong.D: Paper was cheaper than many older materials, not costlier.

questions.stem: Why did China keep the craft a secret for a long time?
options: No one else in the world ever wanted to learn it
It kept a valuable skill special to China
Other faraway lands already knew how to make fine paper
Paper was not useful to anybody at all back then
questions.why: Keeping the craft close to home let China hold on to a valuable skill that few others knew.

wrong.A: The craft later spread, which shows others wanted it.
wrong.C: Other lands did not yet know the craft at first.
wrong.D: The article shows paper became very useful everywhere.

questions.stem: How did the craft of papermaking travel from China toward the west?
options: It traveled only by sea in giant wooden ships
Traders carried it along old trade roads west
It was never shared with anyone outside of China
It was lost completely and reinvented in every new place
questions.why: The article says traders carried the skill west along trade roads, reaching cities such as Samarkand.

wrong.A: Only ships are not mentioned; the article names trade roads.
wrong.C: The article says the craft did spread outside China.
wrong.D: The craft was passed on and learned, not reinvented each time.

HIGH.prompt: How did papermaking change as it moved from China through the Islamic world and into Europe? Support your answer with evidence from the article.
checklist: I explained at least two ways papermaking changed as it spread.
I connected the changes to specific regions, such as China, Samarkand, or Spain.
I used precise words such as technique, adapt, and innovation.
HIGH.modelAnswer: Papermaking began in China, where workers refined an existing technique using cloth, bark, and plant fiber to form pulp that could be pressed and dried into sheets. As the craft moved west along trade routes to Samarkand, and later into the Islamic world's great cities such as Baghdad and Damascus, local artisans had to adapt the process to their own materials, often using linen rags and flowing river water to refine the pulp into stronger, smoother paper. By the time this innovation reached Spain and then Italy, each region had added its own exchange of ideas and small improvements, leaving behind a shared legacy that no single country could claim entirely for itself.
